title: The server gets slow every afternoon, and its own CPU graph says it's idle
intro: The reporting server slows to a crawl every day from about 14:00 until evening. Commands take seconds to respond. The team's dashboard shows the application using only 20 to 30% CPU at those times, so they've ruled CPU out and spent two days looking at the database. The server is an EC2 instance, i-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890, of type t3.medium. It's 15:00 and it's slow now.

steps.prompt: Look at the CPU from the operating system's side, per processor, three one-second samples.

%steal is 74%. The application gets 18% and wants far more: only 3% is idle. Steal is time the virtual machine was ready to run and the hypervisor gave the physical CPU to something else. On a t3 instance that points one way. Check the instance's CPU credit balance over the last hour (a saved query is in credits.json).
Zero credits. Confirm how the instance is set to behave when it runs out: show its credit specification.

'standard': with no credits left, the instance is throttled to its baseline, 20% of each CPU for a t3.medium. That's the wall it hits at 14:00 each day once the morning's reports have spent the credits. To stop the throttling right now, switch the instance to unlimited mode.

Steal is gone and the application is using 84% of both CPUs: that's its real demand. What does that tell you about the instance type?
  a) Nothing
  b) A workload that needs most of the CPU for hours each day is the wrong fit for a burstable instance: it should run on a fixed-performance type (m or c family), which will also cost less than paying for unlimited credits daily
  c) It needs a t3.micro
  d) The application has a bug
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
t3.medium   : baseline 20% per vCPU, earns credits when idle, spends them above baseline
this job    : ~85% for 6 hours a day -> spends far more than it earns
unlimited   : keeps running, billed for the surplus credits
m7g / c7g   : 100% of each vCPU, all the time, at a flat price
steps.hint: Burstable instances are priced for workloads that are idle most of the time.

resolution: The dashboard wasn't lying; it was answering a different question. It showed the application using 20 to 30% of the CPU, which was true, because 20% is all the instance was being allowed. A t3 instance is burstable: it's entitled to a baseline (20% per vCPU for a t3.medium), earns credits while it runs below that, and spends them to run above it. The reporting jobs start in the morning and run flat out; by early afternoon the credits are gone, and in 'standard' mode the hypervisor then holds the instance to its baseline. From inside the machine that appears as steal time: the virtual CPU was ready to work and wasn't given the physical one. %steal at 74% is the unmistakable sign, and it's a column most dashboards don't show, which is how two days went into investigating a healthy database. The same number rises on any virtualised host when a noisy neighbour, or an overcommitted hypervisor, takes your time. Unlimited mode removed the throttle at once, and the next reading showed the truth: the workload wants about 85% of two CPUs for hours. That's not a bursty workload, so the real fix is a fixed-performance instance type, which will be both faster and cheaper than buying surplus credits every afternoon. Lessons: graph steal alongside user and system time, always; for burstable instances, alert on CPUCreditBalance approaching zero; and when a machine is slow while 'not using much CPU', ask what limit could be holding it there. Container CPU limits do the same thing through throttling, visible in the cgroup's nr_throttled counter rather than in steal.
